title: The Half-Light Inventory
premise: Ines Quintana has tuned pianos in the same fading neighborhood for twenty years, listening through the radiators to the arguments, lullabies, and silences of the building he can never bring himself to leave — or to speak honestly within. When Aurelia Sanch, the last fluent speaker of a dying language, asks him to become her final student, he is drawn into a race against rerouted buses, gentrifying developers, and his own lifelong habit of almost saying what matters. As the old neighborhood's last bus line is scheduled for permanent rerouting, Ines must finally choose between loyalty to the people who raised him and the truth he owes them. The novel ends with Ines speaking goodbye aloud in Aurelia's language at the final stop, having recorded her voice but lost the chance to save either her language or his own unspoken love.
about_author: Ulyana Dravenmoor is the pen name of a former radio archivist who spent a decade recording disappearing dialects across coastal cities before turning to fiction. She writes from a converted tram depot, where she claims the heating pipes still carry conversations from 1974.

chapters.title: The Radiator Archive
chapters.summary: Ines, tuning a piano in the building where he grew up, hears through the pipes an argument between his aging landlady Marta and a developer's surveyor. His POV establishes his gift for listening and his cowardice with words; he overhears Marta defending him to strangers and says nothing. Emotional beat: tender shame, the comfort of eavesdropping as a substitute for intimacy.

chapters.title: Aurelia Sanch Requests a Student
chapters.summary: Aurelia, ninety-one and the last speaker of Vessic, summons Ines — she heard him humming a Vessic counting song while working and believes the language chose him. Told partly from Aurelia's POV, the chapter shows her ruthless clarity about death versus his evasiveness. Beat: reluctant hope; Ines accepts not out of passion but because refusing would require saying something true.

chapters.title: Lessons in Almost
chapters.summary: First lessons: Aurelia teaches through objects in her apartment, each word tied to a thing that will outlive them both. Ines's POV alternates with flashbacks to his mother, who spoke Vessic and died mid-sentence with him. He practices vocabulary but deflects when Aurelia asks why he never learned from his mother. Beat: grief surfacing under discipline.

chapters.title: The Rerouting Notice
chapters.summary: The city announces the 47 bus — the neighborhood's artery — will be permanently rerouted in six weeks. Marta's POV reveals she has secretly signed papers selling the building, believing Ines will finally move on. Ines discovers the notice taped inside the bus shelter and cannot tell Marta he knows. Beat: dread compounding silence; loyalty beginning to curdle into complicity.

chapters.title: What the Pipes Carried
chapters.summary: Ines tunes the developer's model-unit piano as a paid spy job and hears, through new thin walls, nothing — the soundproofing erases history. Realizing what the neighborhood loses, he copies Marta's sale documents while there. His POV; the beat is corruption's first taste: he tells himself he stole the papers to protect Marta, but he wants leverage.

chapters.title: Aurelia's Bargain
chapters.summary: Aurelia collapses mid-lesson; in the hospital she offers Ines a deal — record every word she knows, but only if he promises to speak one full sentence of Vessic aloud in public before she dies. Her POV dominates, fierce and unsentimental. Ines agrees without understanding the sentence must be his own. Beat: love against duty, the debt becoming explicit.

chapters.title: The Recording Sessions
chapters.summary: Ines records Aurelia nightly, hoarding hours of her voice like currency, while using the stolen documents to stall the building sale behind Marta's back. Marta's POV catches him lying about where he goes each evening. Rising tension: his secrets multiply — the theft, the lessons, the feelings for Marta's late son he never mourned openly. Beat: power corrupting the gentle.

chapters.title: Marta Reads the Papers
chapters.summary: Marta finds the copied documents and understands Ines has known everything — the sale, the betrayal of her trust — and said nothing, again. Confrontation in the boiler room where the pipes scream heat. She calls him a man who listens so he never has to answer. His POV shatters. Beat: climax of the loyalty-versus-truth theme; the relationship breaks open.

chapters.title: The Last Full Sentence
chapters.summary: Aurelia, dying, refuses to continue recordings until Ines composes his sentence. Alone at night he writes it in Vessic: a goodbye to his mother, an apology to Marta, a confession that he chose silence over love for twenty years. Climax: he speaks it aloud, badly, alone in the stairwell — and the building seems to hold its breath. Beat: terror, then unbearable relief.

chapters.title: Final Stop
chapters.summary: Aurelia dies at dawn; Ines plays her recordings on the last run of the 47 bus before rerouting, speaking the goodbye properly, out loud, at the old terminus. Marta rides beside him; they do not reconcile fully, but they begin. Resolution: the language survives in one student and one honest sentence — enough, the novel argues, to be a legacy. Beat: elegiac peace, grief spoken rather than stored.
